summary: S5 is a low-density nano-bainitic Al–C steel (0.60 wt.% C, 3.92 wt.% Al, with 0.78 wt.% Ni) from a five-steel study on high-C–Al low-density bainitic grades. This sample was austenitized at TA = 1150 °C for 15 min (10 K/s), cooled at 100 K/s and austempered at TB = 335 °C for 700 s — the lower of the two austempering temperatures applied to S5 and only ~4 °C above its measured Ms of 331 °C. The study question was how C–Al alloy level and austempering temperature govern bainitic transformation kinetics and the resulting strength–ductility balance; S5, with the leanest C–Al design, showed the fastest bainitic transformation of the whole set (700–1000 s) and a fine bainitic microstructure with virtually no sheaf impingement.
composition: Nominal chemical composition of alloy S5 (wt.%, Fe balance): C 0.60, Al 3.92, Mn 1.01, Si 0.31, Mo 0.50, Ni 0.78; B and Ti were not deliberately added (dashes in the composition table). The alloy was designed as a "lower alloying concept" within the study: Al at 3.92 wt.% is well below the 5.8–8 wt.% used in S1–S4, and C is reduced to 0.60 wt.% to accelerate the bainitic transformation and mitigate brittleness. Al serves as the density-reducing and ferrite-stabilizing element that accelerates bainitic transformation, while Si is kept low (0.31 wt.%) because Al also suppresses carbide precipitation; Mo is present for hardenability. Ni (0.78 wt.%) is added in place of higher Mn to promote an αp-free (polygonal-ferrite-free) microstructure without compromising bainitic transformation kinetics or reducing strength, its content being minimized because of cost and its austenite-stabilizing effect.
processing: Route: vacuum arc furnace casting of the steel block → homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to promote uniform composition and microstructure → step-by-step hot rolling with thickness reduced to ~11 mm, followed by slow cooling in the oven → sample fabrication by water jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, WA, USA) to precise geometries with minimal thermal distortion. Cylindrical specimens (ø5 × 10 mm³) were heat treated in a DIL 805A dilatometer (TA Instruments): heating at 10 K/s to the austenitizing temperature TA = 1150 °C with a 15 min isothermal hold, then controlled cooling at 100 K/s — fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations and ensure a fine bainitic transformation — down to the austempering temperature TB = 335 °C, followed by an isothermal bainitic hold of 700 s (the Bt determined from dilatometry) and final cooling. TA = 1150 °C is the fixed austenitizing temperature applied to S1, S2, S4 and S5 to allow consistent comparison; for S5 it is the optimized value above the measured operational TA (~900 °C) and the MatCalc ferrite-free TA (986 °C), giving advanced carbide dissolution and suppressing αp to a very small residual fraction (≲1 %). TB = 335 °C is the lower of the two S5 austempering temperatures (335 °C and 365 °C) and lies ~4 °C above the measured Ms = 331 °C of S5.
microstructure: Austempering S5 at 335 °C produced a predominantly bainitic microstructure with four phases. The dominant bainitic ferrite (α, bcc) forms a fine, well-connected lamellar network arranged in narrow packets with intra-packet orientation clustering, separated by frequent high-angle packet/block boundaries; the true lamellar thickness is Lt(t) = 41 nm with a standard deviation SD(Lt(t)) = 14 nm — the most refined condition studied for S5. Retained austenite is present at 19 vol.% (XRD/Rietveld), predominantly film-like at bainite lath boundaries. Lenticular martensite occurs only sporadically (fine bainitic lamellae are seen wrapped inside larger martensite units) and lies below XRD detectability — no martensite reflection is resolvable in XRD (41–46° 2θ). A trace of polygonal ferrite (<1.0 %) remains, seen on grain boundaries in SEM. No SEM-resolvable (Fe,M)xCy precipitates were found after austempering, consistent with the lean alloying level and the TTP assessment, and the relatively symmetric XRD peak shapes indicate limited precipitation-induced broadening. Phase micro-strains are εγ = 0.51 % (austenite) and εα = 0.45 % (ferrite). EBSD shows bands of elevated local misorientation (KAM) along lath/packet boundaries and at sheaf tips, with local KAM hot-spots adjacent to the sporadic martensite plates; the mean KAM is ~0.825° (median 0.692°). Because the film-like γr is near or below the EBSD step size (0.2 μm), EBSD under-counts retained austenite relative to XRD, and XRD is therefore taken as quantitative for phase fractions. Relative to the 365 °C condition, lowering TB to 335 °C refines the bainitic plates, concentrates local lattice curvature near martensite and lath interfaces, and reduces and stiffens the retained austenite.
properties: Tensile testing on ASTM E8 sub-size round specimens (12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length) in a Zwick/Roell universal testing machine (250 kN load cell) gave, for S5 austenitized at 1150 °C and austempered at 335 °C, an ultimate tensile strength of 1530 MPa with 7.0 % total elongation, i.e. a PSE (product of strength and elongation) of 10,710 MPa·%. Bulk hardness was 493 HV30. Compared with the same alloy austempered at 365 °C (UTS 1315 MPa, El 8.7 %, PSE 11,450 MPa·%), the lower TB raises strength at the expense of ductility. For context, S5's UTS–El performance sits intermediate between literature steels containing ≈3 wt.% Al (UTS 1400–2000 MPa, El 9–12 %) and ≈5 wt.% Al (UTS 1300–1850 MPa, El 4–9.5 %), at comparatively higher C contents (0.67–0.94 wt.%). Characterization techniques applied to this sample: dilatometry (DIL 805A) for TA, Ms and transformation kinetics; light optical microscopy (LOM, 6 % Nital etching); scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with EDX; electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, 20 kV, 0.2 μm step size) for IPF and KAM maps; X-ray diffraction (Cu Kα, 40 kV/40 mA, PIXcel 1D detector) with Rietveld refinement for retained-austenite fraction and micro-strain following ASTM E975-13; tensile testing per ASTM E8; and MatCalc equilibrium/TTP precipitation simulations.
mechanisms: Lean C–Al chemistry → fastest transformation: with only 0.60 wt.% C and 3.92 wt.% Al, S5 reached near-complete bainitic transformation in 700 s at 335 °C (and 1000 s at 365 °C), the fastest of all five steels; reducing C weakens austenite stabilization (carbon is known to stabilize austenite and delay transformation), while ~3.92 wt.% Al is described as a near-stoichiometric level giving optimal transformation kinetics.

Ni addition and transformation kinetics: the 0.78 wt.% Ni addition kept the polygonal-ferrite content minimal through austenite stabilization without adversely affecting bainitic transformation kinetics or reducing strength.

Austempering just above Ms → mostly martensite-free structure with sporadic stress-assisted martensite: TB = 335 °C lies ~4 °C above the measured Ms of 331 °C, which suppresses martensite formation during the isothermal hold, yet sporadic lenticular plates still appear because Ms is distributed at the microscale — stress-assisted transformation occurring at local thermal/compositional heterogeneities.

Low-temperature displacive growth → local KAM hot-spots: the sporadic lenticular martensite and the fine lath interfaces generate a high density of geometrically necessary dislocations, producing local misorientation (KAM) maxima adjacent to the martensite plates and elevated-misorientation bands along lath/packet boundaries and sheaf tips.

Lowering TB 365 → 335 °C → finer plates, lower and stiffer retained austenite: the drop in austempering temperature refines bainitic plates (Lt(t) 41 vs 55 nm), reduces the retained-austenite fraction (19 % vs ~26 %) and raises the austenite micro-strain (εγ 0.51 % vs 0.42 %, with the phases diverging from a converged ~0.42–0.43 % at 365 °C); finer plates and concentrated defect fields raise strength, while the smaller γr fraction limits TRIP-assisted strain hardening — explaining the higher UTS (1530 MPa) but lower elongation (7.0 %) at 335 °C versus 1315 MPa/8.7 % at 365 °C.

Lean alloying → minimal sheaf impingement: the moderate Al–C level plus small Ni addition produces a fine, well-connected bainitic ferrite network with minimal impingement of bainite sheaves, which is why S5 transforms fast and cleanly (in contrast to the Ti-microalloyed S4, where impingement limits further acceleration).

COOLING 100 K/s from austenitization: this rate is sufficiently fast to suppress intermediate phase transformations between austenitization and the austempering hold, ensuring the fine bainitic transformation observed.

Absence of SEM-resolvable (Fe,M)xCy after austempering: in line with the TTP simulations for the lean S5 chemistry and the low alloying level, no coarse (Fe,M)xCy precipitates were resolved after the bainitic hold, and the symmetric XRD peak shapes indicate limited precipitation-induced broadening.
conclusions: Within the study's five-steel comparison, S5 represents the "lower C–Al alloying approach" and delivered the fastest bainitic transformation of the set (Bt = 700–1000 s), attributed to its reduced C (0.60 wt.%) and moderate Al (3.92 wt.%) content, with 0.78 wt.% Ni keeping polygonal ferrite at trace level without harming kinetics. When austempered just above its Ms (TB 335 °C, Ms 331 °C), S5 developed very narrow bainitic-ferrite lath packets with only sparse lenticular martensite and localized misorientation hot-spots at lath/martensite interfaces, yielding the fastest transformation (700 s) together with high strength (UTS 1530 MPa) at the expense of ductility (El 7 %), i.e. PSE ≈ 10.7 GPa·% (11.5 GPa·% at 365 °C). Overall the study concludes that TB primarily tunes the UTS–El trade-off via plate thickness and retained-austenite stability, while the 8.08 wt.% Al design (S3) is detrimental to ductility at low TB; S5's rapid transformation and clean interface network are the mechanism by which TB sets the γr/KAM balance without complications from extensive sheaf impingement or secondary precipitation.
unmapped: S5 was one of five low-density Al–C steels (S1–S5) cast, homogenized and hot rolled under an identical prior-processing route, so the reported chemistry and heat-treatment comparison isolates the effect of C–Al level and austempering temperature rather than prior processing; the fixed TA = 1150 °C was chosen for S1, S2, S4 and S5 specifically so that differences in transformation behaviour are attributable to composition and TB.

MatCalc was used to compute ferrite-free TA (986 °C for S5) and carbide-dissolution temperature (Tcd ≈ 775 °C for S5, the lowest of the five steels), and TTP diagrams were simulated at a 100 K/s cooling rate.

For S5, EBSD-derived KAM values are step-size sensitive (maps acquired at different magnifications, 25kx vs 20kx for the 335 °C and 365 °C conditions), so small differences in absolute KAM values should be interpreted with this measurement sensitivity in mind.
